title: Backstage on the workstation
objectives: Select process launches on an exact actor host.
Use a bounded suffix regex with nocase.
Distinguish process presence from execution intent and maliciousness.
story: MIDNIGHT AT MERIDIAN / CHAPTER 3 — The show technician points to the publishing workstation. Rafi says a PowerShell window was 'just the sponsor update.' Jules says the console runs scripts every night. Both explanations are possible. Find the host's process records before turning a familiar tool into a verdict, then cover both PowerShell executable names without searching every workstation.

teaching.heading: A host is another pivot
teaching.text: [HOST] is a stand-in, not an actual computer name. Choose a permitted host inside SecOps and substitute it only there. Keep PROCESS_LAUNCH as the event category.

teaching.heading: A path is text, not a verdict
teaching.text: A filename ending in powershell.exe can be ordinary administration. Querying that path does not run the program or prove it is malicious.

teaching.heading: Read a supplied pattern before changing it
teaching.text: The provided pattern uses a backslash for a Windows path, an escaped dot for a literal period and $ for the end of the path. nocase ignores letter case. The mission explains the exact pattern.

teaching.heading: Two names can share one boundary
teaching.text: Parentheses and a vertical bar inside the supplied regex mean either shell name. Keep the event category and host filter outside that alternative. This is different from a KQL pipeline.

teaching.heading: Useful tools can serve either side
teaching.text: PowerShell is an administration tool and can also be abused. Its name is a lead, not proof of malware. A useful next check is the command line, parent process, account and expected maintenance context, reviewed only inside approved investigation tools.

challenges.title: Find the supplied shell path
challenges.prompt: Select PROCESS_LAUNCH events on principal.hostname [HOST], with target.process.file.full_path ending in a Windows path suffix \\powershell.exe, case-insensitive. Return event rows.
hints: Keep event category and host scope before selecting a process pattern.
Choose the Windows PowerShell suffix pattern and enable nocase; the end anchor matters.

methodQuestions.prompt: What does the final $ in the supplied regex require?

options.label: The filename may occur anywhere in the path.
The filename must be the first directory in the path.
The matched filename must be at the end of the path.

methodQuestions.rationale: The $ anchor closes the suffix match. Without it, additional trailing text could still match.

methodQuestions.prompt: What does nocase change in this process-path filter?

options.label: Letter case no longer affects whether the supplied pattern matches.
The regex becomes an exact string comparison.

methodQuestions.rationale: nocase affects letter case. The pattern and its anchors still apply.

mission.beat: The publishing workstation can push content to the dome. Its operator recalls a PowerShell window during setup. Use the supplied host and executable-path pattern to locate that process category.

explanation.meaning: Keep the search on the requested actor host.
The process path requested by this training task. Check its mapping in your source.
Match a Windows separator, a literal dot and the end of the path.
Match filename letters regardless of case.

mission.remember: A path pattern finds text. It does not prove intent.
mission.caseUpdate: Case clue: the technician says scripts normally load show assets. A shell name alone cannot distinguish maintenance from misuse. Compare its context before making a claim.
mission.caveat: Use existing authorized telemetry. Never execute a command just to create a training match.

analystNote.text: PowerShell supports legitimate administration and can be abused. The host and process record are a starting point. Command line, parent process, account and change approval help explain why it ran.

challenges.title: Allow a second shell name
challenges.prompt: Select PROCESS_LAUNCH events on [HOST] whose target process path ends with either \\powershell.exe or \\pwsh.exe, case-insensitive. Both alternatives must stay inside the event/host scope.
acceptedVariants:
metadata.event_type = "PROCESS_LAUNCH" AND principal.hostname = "__HOST__" AND
(target.process.file.full_path = /\\powershell\.exe$/ nocase OR target.process.file.full_path = /\\pwsh\.exe$/ nocase)
hints: The two shell names are alternatives; host and event type remain required.
Use the predefined combined suffix pattern or an OR of the two suffix patterns.

methodQuestions.prompt: How does /powershell/ differ from the supplied anchored suffix pattern?

options.label: It can match that text within a longer path or filename.
It requires the same Windows separator and .exe suffix.
It matches only the beginning of the path.

methodQuestions.rationale: The shorter unanchored regex does not enforce the supplied separator, literal dot, filename suffix or end boundary.

methodQuestions.prompt: Which change keeps both shell alternatives restricted to the requested host?

options.label: Apply the host filter only to powershell, then OR pwsh outside the group.
Keep the host filter AND the grouped shell alternatives.
Replace the host filter with OR before the shell group.

methodQuestions.rationale: Keep common category/host requirements outside and ANDed with the parenthesized alternatives.

mission.beat: The sponsor guide mentions pwsh.exe as well as powershell.exe. Expand the filename alternative while keeping the host boundary. Do not widen the hunt to every process ending in exe.

explanation.meaning: Inside this provided regex, | means either name.
Keep the end-of-path boundary; an unanchored substring is a different search.
Both shell alternatives must remain in scope.

mission.remember: Change the name choice, not the investigation boundary.
mission.caseUpdate: Case clue: the update guide uses both PowerShell names. You have covered the stated variants without declaring either malicious. Next, check the network lead from the support card.
mission.caveat: The course recognizes only its supplied RE2 patterns and does not execute regex against events.

analystNote.text: A narrow pattern can miss a known variant; a loose one can admit unrelated names. Change only the part your evidence justifies and keep the surrounding constraints.
